newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: China to assist Ivory Coast in oil/gas search.
newsitem.headline: China to assist Ivory Coast in oil/gas search.

text.p: China will help Ivory Coast look for onshore oil and gas along part of its coastline from August, Ivorian Mines and Energy Minister Lamine Fadika said.
"Next month, we plan to start onshore seismic data collection with Chinese cooperation," Fadika told the government daily Fraternite Matin in an interview published on Wednesday.
Exploration would concentrate on an east-west coastal strip from Aboisso to Sassandra -- close to offshore oil and gas fields already on stream or under evaluation.

Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, aims to broaden its farm-based economy by the year 2005 so that oil, gas and mining account for 25-30 percent of Gross Domestic Product, he said. Agriculture is currently 33 percent.
Offshore fields yield 20,000 barrels of oil per day but Fadika said a range of projects were in line to turn Ivory Coast into a "Singapore of Africa" for oil refining and marketing.

National refiner Societe Ivoirienne de Raffinage (SIR) would be further opened up to international investors as part of a $2 billion expansion plan for a new refinery with an annual capacity of 10 million tonnes of crude, he said.
Plans for further privatisation of SIR, slated for late 1997, would proceed although the government, which holds 47 percent of the stock, would retain a significant stake.

Fadika said plans for deepwater oil and gas development would benefit national oil firm Petroci which has recently been restructured into exploration, gas and industrial units under a holding company and opened up to foreign investment.

"From 1998 the three subsidiaries will get a strong boost as deepwater drilling starts and seismic surveys are completed offshore," he said. "French, Canadian, American, Italian, Moroccan and Korean (firms) are already lining up and we have had their written interest in taking a share in these new structures."
Fadika said steps would be taken to avoid conflict in future between local authorities and private oil and gas operators.

U.S.-based United Meridian briefly lost gas production off the south coast town of Jacqueville after authorities there protested that local social projects promised in connection with offshore production had not been met.
"I think the words "Ogoni Syndrome" are excesive in our case," Fadika said, referring to a conflict between Nigeria's Ogoni tribe and oil developers.

"Such incidents discourage investment and should not happen again," he said. "The operating company, under pressure from local populations, had made promises although it is up to the government...to make social investments."

Fadika said the state mining agency Sodemi would also be restructured to encourage more exploration. Around 60 permits have already been issued against a background of complaints about delays in delivering the permits.
"A redefinition of (SODEMI's) purpose and mission" was needed, Fadika said, adding that some mining firms had met permit delays because their application had been imcomplete.
